title: White Hat Hacker

description.intro:
You are trying to hack into an account (for good reasons, I'm sure). You know that the password:

has at least 1 and at most 10 letters,
uses only lowercase English letters,
does not repeat any letter.
You have a script that tries to log in with a given password and returns a boolean indicating if it was successful. Write a function to find the password. You can call check_password(s) to check if s is the password.

Example:
check_password("a")   # returns False
check_password("abc") # returns False
check_password("ac")  # returns False
check_password("ab")  # returns False
check_password("bc")  # returns True
Output: "bc"
description.approach:
There is no explicit limit to how many times you can call check_password().

The fact that the "password size" is 10 is a trigger to use backtracking.

We can model backtracking algorithms as doing a DFS through a decision tree.

In this case:

The root is the empty string.
At each step, we decide which letter to add next. We consider only letters that haven't been used yet.
The leaves are strings of length 10, as that is the maximum length.
One special feature about this decision tree is that non-leaf nodes are also potential passwords, as the password may have fewer than 10 letters. Thus, we also call check_password() for internal nodes, not only at the leaves.

We use the backtracking recipe:

def visit(partial_solution):
  if full_solution(partial_solution):
    # Process leaf/full solution.
  else:
    for choice in choices(partial_solution):
      # Prune children where possible.
      child = apply_choice(partial_solution)
      visit(child)

visit(empty_solution)

complexity:
Time & Space Analysis
In the worst case, the number of check_password() calls will be 26 * 25 * 24 * ... * 17, which is approximately 2 * 10^13 = O(1). Since there is no input size variable, the runtime is constant.

Time: O(1)
Extra space: O(1)
Fun fact: assuming that we call the script one million times per second, it would take approximately 223 days to try them all, but we can check all passwords of length up to 8 in less than one day. That's why short passwords are a bad idea!

We could also analyze the runtime in terms of the maximum length of the password. If we call it n (n = 10 in the specific case of this problem), the runtime is O(26! / (26 - n)!).

tests.python:
def run_tests():

  def check_password_factory(correct_password):
    return lambda s: s == correct_password

  tests = [
      "a",
      "bc",
      "def",
      "ghij",
      # Try higher numbers if you'd like to see how fast this stops working
      # but you'll need to edit the max_length variable in the find_password
      # function to make it longer. 8 characters may take a long time to run.
      # "klmno",
      # "pqrstu",
      # "vwxyzab"
  ]
  for correct_password in tests:
    check_password = check_password_factory(correct_password)
    got = find_password(check_password, 4)
    assert got == correct_password, f"\nfind_password({correct_password}): got: {        got}, want: {correct_password}\n"

run_tests()
